title: Colonial Egypt and the Monarchy
subtitle: 1900–1952 · The Protectorate, the 1919 Revolution, the Liberal Experiment, and the Fall of the Monarchy

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Protectorate, the 1919 revolution, the constitutional monarchy, and the three-way struggle of Palace, Wafd and Britain to the 1952 coup

entries.label: Abbas II Hilmi — deposed
entries.hint: Abbas II spent the two decades of Cromer's rule chafing against it and cultivating the nationalist press. When the Ottoman Empire entered the First World War on Germany's side in November 1914, Britain declared a Protectorate over Egypt, severed the Ottoman link, and deposed Abbas — who was in Istanbul — for his pro-Ottoman sympathies. He never returned; his uncle was installed in his place with a new title.
entries.note: P.J. Vatikiotis, The History of Modern Egypt (4th ed. 1991) pp.240–47. The Protectorate proclamation, 18 December 1914; the deposition, 19 December 1914 (British official gazette).

entries.label: Sultan Husayn Kamil
entries.hint: Britain gave the throne to Husayn Kamil, a son of Ismaʿil, with the title 'Sultan of Egypt' — a deliberate assertion that Egypt was no longer, even nominally, an Ottoman viceroyalty. He reigned under martial law through the hardest years of the war, the target of two assassination attempts, and died in October 1917. The crown passed to his brother Ahmad Fuad rather than to his own son, who declined the offer of a throne 'held by grace of the British'.
entries.note: Vatikiotis, The History of Modern Egypt (1991) pp.246–49. The title change: the British High Commission records; M.W. Daly (ed.), The Cambridge History of Egypt, vol.2 (1998) ch. 10.

entries.label: Fuad I
entries.hint: Fuad was the dominant royal figure of the constitutional monarchy — autocratic, distrustful of the Wafd's mass following, and determined to make the Palace the real centre of power. He used the 1923 constitution's grant of the right to dissolve parliament and appoint governments to keep the elected Wafd majority out of office for most of his reign, ruling through minority ministries and, under Sidqi in 1930–33, a suspended constitution. He also pursued the caliphate for himself and founded the national university.
entries.note: Afaf Lutfi al-Sayyid Marsot, Egypt's Liberal Experiment 1922–1936 (1977). The 1926 Caliphate Congress: Elie Kedourie, 'Egypt and the Caliphate 1915–52', in The Chatham House Version (1970).

entries.label: Farouk I
entries.hint: Farouk came to the throne at sixteen, briefly popular as a young, pious, Egyptian-educated king. His reign was consumed by his feud with the Wafd, his manoeuvring against the British, and, after the war, by scandal — the corruption of the court, the arms procured for the failed Palestine campaign, his lifestyle. The humiliation of 4 February 1942, when British tanks forced him to accept a government, damaged him lastingly. The Free Officers deposed him on 26 July 1952, and he sailed into exile from Alexandria.
entries.note: Vatikiotis, The History of Modern Egypt (1991); Barrie St Clair McBride, Farouk of Egypt (1967); Selma Botman, Egypt from Independence to Revolution 1919–1952 (1991).

entries.label: The man in the Residency
entries.hint: Britain's chief representative — Consul-General to 1914, High Commissioner under the Protectorate, Ambassador after 1936 — remained the decisive figure in Egyptian politics for the whole period. Cromer gave way to Gorst and Kitchener; Allenby forced through the 1922 declaration and issued the Stack ultimatum; Lampson (Lord Killearn) delivered the 1942 ultimatum to Farouk. Even after the 1936 Treaty converted 'occupation' into 'alliance', the ambassador's word carried the weight of an army in the Canal Zone.
entries.note: John Darwin, Britain, Egypt and the Middle East (1981); Roger Owen, Lord Cromer (2004). Lampson's diaries: The Killearn Diaries 1934–1946 (ed. Trefor Evans, 1972).

entries.label: Butros Ghali and the assassination of 1910
entries.hint: Butros Ghali Pasha, a Copt, was Prime Minister from 1908, and in office signed the 1899 Sudan condominium's revision, revived the Press Law of 1881 to muzzle the nationalist papers, and reopened the question of extending the Suez Canal Company's concession. In February 1910 he was shot dead by a young nationalist, Ibrahim al-Wardani. The killing — a Muslim nationalist murdering a Coptic premier — inflamed sectarian feeling and split opinion about the National Party's methods.
entries.note: Malak Badrawi, Political Violence in Egypt 1910–1925: Secret Societies, Plots and Assassinations (2000); B.L. Carter, The Copts in Egyptian Politics 1918–1952 (1986) pp.5–20.

entries.label: Zaghlul's government of 1924
entries.hint: Egypt's first free general election under the 1923 constitution gave the Wafd 179 of 214 seats, and Saʿd Zaghlul became Prime Minister in January 1924. His government pressed Britain on the reserved points — full independence, the Sudan, the withdrawal of troops — and got nowhere in London. After Sir Lee Stack was assassinated in Cairo in November and Britain responded with a punishing ultimatum, Zaghlul resigned rather than enforce it. The first Wafd government had lasted ten months.
entries.note: Marius Deeb, Party Politics in Egypt: The Wafd and its Rivals 1919–1939 (1979); Marsot, Egypt's Liberal Experiment (1977) pp.99–120. The 1924 election results.

entries.label: The palace and minority ministries
entries.hint: Whenever the Wafd won an election, the King, with British acquiescence, found a way to keep it out of power: parliament dissolved, the constitution amended or suspended, a minority government installed. Ahmad Ziwar governed after Zaghlul; Muhammad Mahmud ruled without parliament in 1928–29; and Ismaʿil Sidqi, from 1930, imposed a new constitution enlarging royal power and governed by decree and repression for three years. The 'liberal experiment' spent most of the decade under unelected governments.
entries.note: Marsot, Egypt's Liberal Experiment 1922–1936 (1977) — the standard account. Sidqi's regime: 'Abd al-'Azim Ramadan, and Sidqi's own memoirs, Mudhakkirati (1950).

entries.label: Mustafa al-Nahhas and the Wafd in office
entries.hint: Nahhas, Zaghlul's successor as Wafd leader, was Prime Minister five times between 1928 and 1952. His 1936 government negotiated the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty; the King dismissed him in 1937. British tanks brought him back to power in February 1942, an intervention that tainted the Wafd. His last government, from 1950, abrogated the 1936 Treaty in October 1951 and was dismissed after the Cairo Fire. The Wafd's repeated failure to convert its majorities into lasting power is central to the collapse of the parliamentary order.
entries.note: Deeb, Party Politics in Egypt (1979); Botman, Egypt from Independence to Revolution (1991). The 1936 Treaty: Vatikiotis, The History of Modern Egypt (1991) pp.284–92.

entries.label: The postwar ministries and the collapse
entries.hint: After the war, governments fell in quick succession amid strikes, demonstrations, a failed treaty negotiation and the Palestine defeat. Mahmud Fahmi al-Nuqrashi (Saʿdist) imposed martial law and dissolved the Muslim Brotherhood in December 1948, and was assassinated by a Brother days later; his successor Ibrahim ʿAbd al-Hadi ran a savage repression in which Hasan al-Banna was killed. The Wafd returned in 1950, abrogated the treaty, lost control of the Canal Zone campaign, and was dismissed after Black Saturday. Four prime ministers held office in the six months before the coup.
entries.note: Botman, Egypt from Independence to Revolution (1991); Joel Gordon, Nasser's Blessed Movement: Egypt's Free Officers and the July Revolution (1992) pp.19–43.

entries.group: The National Movement and Its Rivals
entries.label: Mustafa Kamil and the National Party
entries.hint: Before the war, nationalism meant the young lawyer Mustafa Kamil — his fiery daily al-Liwaʾ, his appeals to the Ottoman Sultan and to French and then German opinion, and the National Party he founded in 1907, the year before his death at 33. The Denshawai hangings of 1906 gave the movement a martyrology and a mass audience, and its slogan was immediate British evacuation. Under his successor Muhammad Farid the party was harried by the Press Law and the deportations and lost ground to the exiled and the underground.
entries.note: Arthur Goldschmidt, 'The Egyptian Nationalist Party 1892–1919', in P.M. Holt (ed.), Political and Social Change in Modern Egypt (1968); Ziad Fahmy, Ordinary Egyptians: Cultivating Dynamic Nationalism (2011) chs. 3–4.

entries.group: The National Movement and Its Rivals
entries.label: Saʿd Zaghlul and the Wafd
entries.hint: On 13 November 1918 Saʿd Zaghlul and two colleagues asked the British to let a delegation — a wafd — put Egypt's case for independence to the Paris Peace Conference. The refusal, and Zaghlul's exile, triggered the 1919 revolution and made the Wafd the national party — a mass organisation with a claim to embody the whole nation, Muslim and Copt, town and country. It won every free election it was allowed to contest and was kept from power for most of the period by the Palace and the British.
entries.note: Deeb, Party Politics in Egypt (1979); Janice Terry, The Wafd 1919–1952 (1982). Zaghlul's diaries: Mudhakkirat Sa'd Zaghlul (ed. 'Abd al-'Azim Ramadan, 1987– ).

entries.group: The National Movement and Its Rivals
entries.label: Hasan al-Banna and the Muslim Brotherhood
entries.hint: The Society of the Muslim Brothers was founded in 1928 at Ismailia by a 22-year-old schoolteacher, Hasan al-Banna, as a movement for moral and social reform on Islamic lines. By the 1940s it had perhaps half a million members and a network of schools, clinics, workshops, scout troops and a clandestine 'special apparatus'. It sent volunteers to Palestine in 1948, was dissolved that December after a spate of political violence, and was implicated in the assassination of Prime Minister Nuqrashi; al-Banna was killed by the security services in February 1949.
entries.note: Richard P. Mitchell, The Society of the Muslim Brothers (1969) — the classic study. Brynjar Lia, The Society of the Muslim Brothers in Egypt 1928–1942 (1998).

entries.group: The National Movement and Its Rivals
entries.label: The radical fringe
entries.hint: Alongside the Wafd and the Brotherhood grew smaller militant movements. Young Egypt (Misr al-Fatat), founded by Ahmad Husayn in 1933 with its Green Shirt paramilitaries, blended ultranationalism, Islam and, at times, admiration for the Axis. Communist circles that had existed since the 1920s were revived and Egyptianised in the 1940s, working among students and factory workers. By the late 1940s Cairo politics ran partly on street violence between these groups, the Brotherhood, and the parties' own strong-arm squads.
entries.note: James Jankowski, Egypt's Young Rebels: 'Young Egypt' 1933–1952 (1975); Selma Botman, The Rise of Egyptian Communism 1939–1970 (1988); Joel Beinin, Was the Red Flag Flying There? (1990).

entries.group: The National Movement and Its Rivals
entries.label: The Free Officers and the coup of 23 July 1952
entries.hint: A clandestine group of junior army officers, organised chiefly by Gamal Abdel Nasser and drawn from men embittered by the 1942 humiliation, the 1948 Palestine defeat and the Canal Zone fighting, seized power in a near-bloodless night operation on 23 July 1952, using General Muhammad Naguib as their public figurehead. A Revolutionary Command Council took over the government; King Farouk abdicated in favour of his infant son and left the country on 26 July. The monarchy was formally abolished in June 1953.
entries.note: Joel Gordon, Nasser's Blessed Movement: Egypt's Free Officers and the July Revolution (1992). The participants' accounts: Anwar Sadat, Revolt on the Nile (1957); Khaled Mohi El Din, Memories of a Revolution (1995).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Denshawai, the 1919 uprising, the two world wars on Egyptian soil, the 1948 Palestine defeat, and the Canal Zone campaign and the Cairo Fire

entries.label: The Denshawai incident
entries.hint: When British officers shooting pigeons near the Delta village of Denshawai set fire to a threshing floor and wounded a woman, villagers attacked them; one officer died, apparently of sunstroke and concussion, while trying to reach his camp. A special tribunal hanged four villagers, flogged others in public, and sentenced more to hard labour. The severity, and the public floggings, provoked an outcry in Egypt and in Britain — George Bernard Shaw wrote a famous indictment — and helped end Cromer's proconsulship the next year.
entries.note: George Bernard Shaw, preface to John Bull's Other Island (1907). Wilfrid Blunt, Atrocities of Justice under British Rule in Egypt (1906). Analysis: Ziad Fahmy, Ordinary Egyptians (2011) pp.84–101.

entries.label: The First World War in Egypt
entries.hint: Egypt spent the war under martial law as a vast British base for the Gallipoli and Palestine campaigns. Ottoman forces twice attacked the Suez Canal and were repulsed. Hundreds of thousands of Egyptian peasants were conscripted — often by the village headman's press-gang — into the Labour Corps and the Camel Transport Corps and sent to the fronts, while animals, grain and cotton were requisitioned and prices soared. The war's exactions did more than any speech to spread nationalist feeling into the villages.
entries.note: Kyle Anderson, The Egyptian Labor Corps: Race, Space, and Place in the First World War (2021); Latifa Salim, Misr fi al-harb al-'alamiyya al-ula (1984). Vatikiotis, The History of Modern Egypt (1991) pp.246–56.

entries.label: The 1919 Revolution
entries.hint: The arrest and deportation of Saʿd Zaghlul and three colleagues to Malta on 8 March 1919 set off a nationwide rising: student and lawyers' strikes in Cairo, railway and telegraph workers cutting communications, crowds attacking British soldiers and installations — several were killed — and an armed rural revolt across the Delta and Middle Egypt. Muslims and Copts marched together; women demonstrated in the streets. The army restored order with heavy force, killing around 800 Egyptians, and Britain released Zaghlul and sent the Milner Mission to negotiate.
entries.note: Ellis Goldberg, 'Peasants in Revolt — Egypt 1919', IJMES 24 (1992); Reinoud Leenders and, definitively, the contemporary British and Egyptian records. Marsot, Egypt's Liberal Experiment (1977) pp.55–78.

entries.label: The assassination of Sir Lee Stack
entries.hint: Sir Lee Stack, Governor-General of the Sudan and commander of the Egyptian army, was shot dead in a Cairo street by nationalist gunmen. High Commissioner Allenby answered with an ultimatum going far beyond the crime: a large indemnity, the immediate withdrawal of all Egyptian troops and officials from the Sudan, and an unlimited expansion of the British irrigation scheme in the Gezira. Zaghlul's government resigned rather than comply; the Wafd's standing and Egypt's position in the Sudan both suffered lasting damage.
entries.note: M.W. Daly, Empire on the Nile: The Anglo-Egyptian Sudan 1898–1934 (1986) ch. 8; Marsot, Egypt's Liberal Experiment (1977) pp.114–20.

entries.label: The Second World War in Egypt
entries.hint: Egypt was neutral in law and a huge Allied base in fact, its ports, airfields, railways and factories turned over to the war. The Western Desert campaign swung back and forth across its territory; in the summer of 1942 Rommel's advance reached El Alamein, about a hundred kilometres from Alexandria, and the British burned their files in Cairo before the two battles of Alamein turned the war. The base spending drove wild inflation and profiteering, and the sight of the war fed both a pro-Axis current and a general contempt for the political class.
entries.note: Artemis Cooper, Cairo in the War 1939–1945 (1989); Robert Vitalis & Steven Heydemann, 'War, Keynesianism, and Colonialism', in Heydemann (ed.), War, Institutions and Social Change in the Middle East (2000).

entries.label: The 4 February 1942 incident
entries.hint: With Rommel advancing and Farouk resisting a Wafd government Britain wanted for its wartime reliability, Ambassador Lampson surrounded Abdin Palace with tanks and infantry and handed the King a choice: appoint Mustafa al-Nahhas Prime Minister within the hour, or abdicate. Farouk signed. The spectacle of the King coerced at gunpoint, and of the Wafd taking office on British armour, discredited both the monarchy and the largest party at a stroke and convinced a group of young officers that the whole order had to go.
entries.note: Charles Tripp, 'Egypt 1945–52: The Uses of Disorder', in Cohen & Kolinsky (eds.), Demise of the British Empire in the Middle East (1998); Laila Amin Morsy, 'The Military Clauses of the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty', IJMES 16 (1984). Lampson's own account in The Killearn Diaries.

entries.label: The 1948 Palestine War
entries.hint: Egypt sent an army into Palestine in May 1948 alongside the other Arab states against the new state of Israel. After early gains the campaign turned into defeat; an Egyptian brigade, with Major Gamal Abdel Nasser among its officers, was besieged for months in the Faluja pocket. Nationalist opinion blamed the loss on royal corruption and 'defective arms' supplied to the army through palace cronies. The armistice of February 1949 left Egypt holding only the Gaza Strip, and the army turned its bitterness on the regime.
entries.note: Fawaz Gerges, 'Egypt and the 1948 War', in Rogan & Shlaim (eds.), The War for Palestine (2001); Gamal Abdel Nasser, Egypt's Liberation: The Philosophy of the Revolution (1955) on Faluja.

entries.group: The End of the Old Order
entries.label: The Canal Zone campaign and the Cairo Fire
entries.hint: After Nahhas unilaterally abrogated the 1936 Treaty in October 1951, a guerrilla campaign against the British base in the Canal Zone was waged by police auxiliaries, students and Brotherhood volunteers with government tolerance. On 25 January 1952 British troops stormed the Ismailia police barracks, killing about fifty. The next day, 'Black Saturday', mobs burned the European centre of Cairo — cinemas, hotels, department stores, Shepheard's — killing dozens. Martial law, four short-lived governments, and then the coup followed within six months.
entries.note: Anne-Claire Kerboeuf, 'The Cairo Fire of 26 January 1952', in Goldschmidt et al. (eds.), Re-Envisioning Egypt 1919–1952 (2005); Joel Gordon, Nasser's Blessed Movement (1992) pp.34–43.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The 1923 constitution and the liberal experiment, the reserved points, the end of the capitulations, and the failure of parliamentary government

entries.label: The Protectorate and the reserved points
entries.hint: Britain ruled Egypt as a formal Protectorate under martial law from December 1914. When the 1919 revolution made that untenable, it issued a unilateral declaration on 28 February 1922 ending the Protectorate and recognising Egypt as 'an independent sovereign state' — while reserving 'absolutely to the discretion of His Majesty's Government' four matters: imperial communications, defence, the protection of foreign interests and minorities, and the Sudan. It was independence with a permanent mortgage on the four things that mattered most.
entries.note: The Declaration to Egypt, 28 February 1922 (Cmd. 1592). John Darwin, Britain, Egypt and the Middle East: Imperial Policy in the Aftermath of War 1918–1922 (1981).

entries.label: The 1923 constitution and the liberal experiment
entries.hint: The 1923 constitution set up a parliamentary monarchy on the Belgian model — a bicameral parliament, an elected Chamber, a cabinet answerable to it. But it also gave the King the power to dissolve parliament and to appoint and dismiss ministers, and Fuad and Farouk used those powers to keep the Wafd majority out of office for most of the period; the constitution itself was suspended from 1930 to 1935 under Sidqi. Between a grasping Palace, an overriding British presence, and a Wafd that could not govern, the 'liberal experiment' never worked as intended.
entries.note: Afaf Lutfi al-Sayyid Marsot, Egypt's Liberal Experiment 1922–1936 (1977) — the title study. The constitution text: al-Waqa'i' al-Misriyya, 20 April 1923.

entries.label: The 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty
entries.hint: Nahhas's government signed a twenty-year treaty of alliance with Britain in August 1936. British forces were to withdraw from the cities to a garrison of up to 10,000 in the Canal Zone; Britain kept the right to reoccupy Egypt in wartime; the Sudan was left as a joint condominium; the High Commissioner became an ambassador; and Britain sponsored Egypt's entry into the League of Nations in 1937. It was the high point of the parliamentary regime's achievement — and, when its terms proved a fig-leaf for continued occupation, a millstone that helped sink the whole order.
entries.note: The Treaty of Alliance, 26 August 1936 (Cmd. 5270). Laila Amin Morsy, 'The Military Clauses of the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of Friendship and Alliance, 1936', IJMES 16 (1984).

entries.label: Montreux and the end of the capitulations
entries.hint: At the Montreux Convention of 1937 the powers agreed to abolish the capitulations — the tax exemptions and legal immunities that had shielded foreign residents since Ottoman times — over a twelve-year transition, at the end of which the Mixed Courts would close. When they did, in 1949, foreigners in Egypt came fully under Egyptian law and taxation for the first time. It was a genuine and hard-won gain in sovereignty, and a heavy blow to the privileged position of the large foreign business communities.
entries.note: The Montreux Convention, 8 May 1937. Nathan Brown, 'The Precarious Life and Slow Death of the Mixed Courts of Egypt', IJMES 25 (1993); Jasper Yeates Brinton, The Mixed Courts of Egypt (rev. ed. 1968).

entries.label: The interventionist state
entries.hint: The state took a growing hand in the economy. Tariff autonomy in 1930 let Egypt protect its infant industries; new ministries and public bodies multiplied; the Second World War brought rationing, price controls and a Supply Ministry; and a modest body of social legislation appeared — limits on child labour and women's hours in 1933, employers' liability in 1936, a wartime minimum wage. The debate over how far the state should plan and own the economy was well underway before 1952.
entries.note: Robert Tignor, State, Private Enterprise, and Economic Change in Egypt 1918–1952 (1984); Ellis Goldberg, Tinker, Tailor, and Textile Worker: Class and Politics in Egypt 1930–1952 (1986).

entries.label: The parties and the rigged election
entries.hint: A multiparty system operated but rarely produced accountable government. The Wafd faced splinters — the Liberal Constitutionalists of 1922, the Saʿdists of 1937 — and the King's own Union Party; every non-Wafd government held elections it won, by managing the rural vote through the provincial administration and the landed notable who controlled his village. Patronage, not policy, ran the party machines, and the Wafd's mass following could not translate into durable power.
entries.note: Marius Deeb, Party Politics in Egypt: The Wafd and its Rivals 1919–1939 (1979); Jacob Landau, Parliaments and Parties in Egypt (1953).

entries.label: The effendi state and the graduate glut
entries.hint: Independence in 1922 brought 'Egyptianisation': British officials were retired and the government schools' graduates — the effendis, in their tarbush and Western suit — filled the bureaucracy. But the schools turned out more graduates than the state and the professions could absorb, and by the 1930s a large class of educated, under-employed or badly paid young men, resentful of the pashas above them and the parties that had failed them, was a political fact. Both the Muslim Brotherhood and the Free Officers recruited heavily from it.
entries.note: Lucie Ryzova, The Age of the Efendiyya: Passages to Modernity in National-Colonial Egypt (2014); Israel Gershoni & James Jankowski, Redefining the Egyptian Nation 1930–1945 (1995).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Islamic modernism and its reaction, the Muslim Brotherhood, the national-unity ideal and its strains, and the al-Azhar reforms

entries.label: Islamic modernism and its reaction
entries.hint: After Muhammad ʿAbduh's death in 1905 his legacy split. Rashid Rida's journal al-Manar carried the reform impulse toward a scripturalist, anti-Sufi salafism. And two controversies marked the limits of liberalisation: in 1925 the Azhar scholar ʿAli ʿAbd al-Raziq argued in Islam and the Foundations of Governance that the caliphate was a political, not a religious, institution and was stripped of his standing; the next year Taha Husayn's book questioning the authenticity of pre-Islamic poetry brought him a prosecution and a public storm.
entries.note: Albert Hourani, Arabic Thought in the Liberal Age 1798–1939 (1962) chs. 9–11; Charles Adams, Islam and Modernism in Egypt (1933); Souad Ali, A Religion, Not a State: Ali Abd al-Raziq's Islamic Justification of Political Secularism (2009).

entries.label: al-Banna's comprehensive Islam
entries.hint: Hasan al-Banna's teaching, spread through the Muslim Brotherhood's lessons, tracts and mass rallies, held that Islam was 'a comprehensive system' — creed, worship, nation, state, economy, and jihad — and that Egypt's ills came from abandoning it for imported models and from the corruption of the political parties. The movement combined personal piety and study circles with schools, clinics, cooperatives and, from the late 1930s, a paramilitary wing. It set the template that Islamist movements across the Muslim world would follow.
entries.note: Hasan al-Banna, Majmuʿat rasaʾil (collected tracts). Richard P. Mitchell, The Society of the Muslim Brothers (1969); Brynjar Lia, The Society of the Muslim Brothers in Egypt (1998).

entries.label: National unity and the Coptic question
entries.hint: The 1919 revolution's emblem was the crescent joined to the cross, and Copts — the Wafd's secretary-general Makram ʿUbayd above all — were central to the national movement and to the ideal of a territorial Egyptian nation above religion. The reality was harder: separate Coptic electorates were debated and rejected in 1923, sectarian incidents recurred, and as public culture turned in the 1930s toward Islam and Arabism many Copts felt their place contracting. The Coptic Congress of 1911 and its grievances echoed through the whole period.
entries.note: B.L. Carter, The Copts in Egyptian Politics 1918–1952 (1986); Paul Sedra, 'Class Cleavages and Ethnic Conflict: Coptic Christian Communities in Modern Egyptian Politics', Islam and Christian–Muslim Relations 10 (1999).

entries.label: al-Azhar between reform and the state
entries.hint: A series of laws in 1911, 1930 and 1936 reorganised al-Azhar into a modern institution with faculties, a fixed curriculum, examinations and degrees, and a rector appointed by the state. The reforms were meant to fit it to compete with the secular university and the government schools; critics said they subordinated the ulama to the government and hollowed out the traditional learning. Al-Azhar's authority was diminished but real — its condemnation could still end a scholar's career, as ʿAbd al-Raziq found.
entries.note: Bayard Dodge, Al-Azhar: A Millennium of Muslim Learning (1961) ch. 8; Indira Falk Gesink, Islamic Reform and Conservatism: Al-Azhar and the Evolution of Modern Sunni Islam (2010).

entries.label: The Sufi orders and the mawlid in the modern city
entries.hint: For the majority, religion still meant the Sufi order, the saint's shrine and the mawlid. The state's Council of Sufi Orders licensed the tariqas and regulated the great festivals; the mawlid of Sayyid al-Badawi at Tanta still drew hundreds of thousands. Both the Islamic modernists and the Muslim Brotherhood attacked this popular Islam as superstition and a mark of backwardness — a class as much as a theological quarrel, the reforming effendi against the practices of the village and the poor quarter.
entries.note: F. de Jong, Turuq and Turuq-Linked Institutions in Nineteenth Century Egypt (1978) and his 20th-century articles; Samuli Schielke, The Perils of Joy: Contesting Mulid Festivals in Contemporary Egypt (2012) for the framing.

entries.label: The Jewish and foreign communities
entries.hint: Egypt's Jewish community reached perhaps 75,000–80,000 by the 1940s, concentrated in Cairo and Alexandria, with its own synagogues, schools, newspapers and welfare bodies, and divided between Zionist, anti-Zionist and simply Egyptian currents. Around it lived large Greek Orthodox, Italian and Maltese Catholic, Armenian and Protestant communities. Together they made Cairo and Alexandria genuinely plural cities — a pluralism that the end of the capitulations, the Palestine war, rising nationalism and, after 1952, the exodus would bring to a close.
entries.note: Gudrun Krämer, The Jews in Modern Egypt 1914–1952 (1989); Joel Beinin, The Dispersion of Egyptian Jewry (1998). The foreign communities: Robert Ilbert & Ilios Yannakakis (eds.), Alexandria 1860–1960 (1997).

timeline.label: The National Movement and Its Rivals
